June 1889. Vincent van Gogh is living at the asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where he went of his own accord to be cared for. From his window he watches the sky before dawn. But the village you have just painted never existed: Vincent invented it, with a steeple that recalls the churches of his native Holland. The cypress, like a dark flame, links the earth to the stars. Today this is one of the most famous paintings in the world. It hangs in New York.

Summer 1889, near Saint-Rémy. Van Gogh sets up his easel in the wind, in front of the ripe wheat. He loves cypresses, which he compares to Egyptian obelisks, and dreams of painting them as no one has before. Look at the clouds: they swirl like the thick paint he lays on with his brush. He loved this landscape so much that he painted three versions. This one is in the National Gallery in London.

Arles, September 1888. Van Gogh spends three nights in this café on Place Lamartine, open at all hours, where drifters sleep. He wants, he writes to his brother Theo, to express the terrible passions of humanity with red and green. The gas lamps throb with yellow halos, the billiard table casts a huge shadow. Vincent called it one of the ugliest pictures he had done, and yet one that mattered most to him.

Spring 1890. Shut away in Saint-Rémy, Van Gogh remembers his youth in northern Europe. He paints cottages with mossy roofs, smoke curling like brushstrokes, a setting sun and a peasant walking home. His letters speak of memories of the North. A few weeks later he will leave Provence for Auvers-sur-Oise, where he paints his very last pictures.

Around 1831, in Japan. Katsushika Hokusai is over seventy when he publishes his Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. This wave is the most famous of them all. Look closely: behind the foam rising like claws, Mount Fuji looks tiny. Three fishing boats dive beneath the crest. Prussian blue, brought from Europe, was then a new colour in Japan. This print was made thousands of times, and it fascinated Monet and Van Gogh alike.

Le Havre, one morning in 1872. Claude Monet paints the harbour from his window: the orange sun shines on the water, the boats are just blue shadows. Two years later he shows it in Paris as Impression, Sunrise. A critic mocks it and calls these painters impressionists. The nickname stuck, and gave its name to a whole movement.

At Giverny, Monet has a pond dug and plants water lilies of every colour. For nearly thirty years he paints this small stretch of water at every hour, in every light: more than two hundred and fifty pictures. There is no bank and no horizon, only the sky reflected between the flowers. Late in life, even as his eyesight failed, he kept painting his water lilies.

Monet settles in Giverny in 1883, in a house surrounded by meadows and poplars. Before creating his famous water garden, he paints the countryside around him, outdoors, in a few quick sessions to catch the light of the moment. Pink trees, grass dotted with flowers: the detail doesn\'t matter, the feeling of a beautiful day does.

Paul Cézanne said he wanted to astonish Paris with an apple. In this still life nothing is quite straight: the table tilts, so does the bottle, and the edge of the cloth doesn\'t line up. It isn\'t clumsiness. Cézanne shows each object from its best angle, as if we were walking around it. Picasso and the cubists would later call him the father of us all. This painting is in Chicago.

Around 1818, in Germany. Caspar David Friedrich paints a man standing on a rock above a sea of clouds. We never see his face, and that is deliberate: we look at the landscape with him, over his shoulder. This wanderer has become the symbol of Romanticism, the movement that sought vastness and emotion in nature. The painting hangs in Hamburg.

Paris, 1872. Pierre-Auguste Renoir settles upstairs in a café facing the Pont-Neuf to paint the crowd in the sun. His brother Edmond helps in his own way: he stops passers-by to ask them the time or the way, while Renoir sketches them. Blue sky, light shadows, strollers: this is the joyful Paris of early impressionism. The painting is now in Washington.

Georges Seurat is twenty-four when he begins this painting. He works on it for two years, laying tiny touches of pure colour side by side. From a distance, our eye blends them: the technique will be called pointillism. On the island of La Grande Jatte, near Paris, Parisians stroll on a Sunday with a monkey, dogs and parasols. The huge original is in Chicago.

In 1832, Eugène Delacroix joins a diplomatic mission to Morocco. In Tangier he attends a Jewish wedding and fills his notebooks with sketches and colours. Back in Paris he paints the scene from memory: the musicians, the dancers, the white light on the walls. That journey changed his painting forever. The picture is in the Louvre.

Around 1658, in Delft, in the Netherlands. Johannes Vermeer paints a maid pouring milk in a quiet kitchen. Look at the light from the window, the little bright dots on the bread, the deep blue of the apron, made from a crushed precious stone, lapis lazuli. Nothing happens, and yet everything seems suspended. Vermeer painted very few pictures, barely forty. This one is in Amsterdam.

Iowa, 1930. Grant Wood notices a small white house with a pointed Gothic window. He imagines the people who might live there, and asks his sister Nan and his dentist to pose. People often think they are husband and wife, but the painter saw them as a father and his daughter. The pitchfork is echoed in the seams of the overalls and in the window. This painting has become one of America\'s best-known images.

Joseph Mallord William Turner, the English painter of light and storms. Here a great ship breaks apart in a raging sea, while small boats try to save the crew. Turner doesn\'t paint every wave: he paints the power of nature, with sweeping gestures and colours that run into each other. More than half a century early, he points the way to the impressionists.

Edvard Munch was walking at sunset near Oslo when, he wrote, the sky turned blood red. He felt, he said, an infinite scream passing through nature. So he painted this figure clutching its head on a bridge, under a sky in flames. Munch made several versions, in paint, pastel and print. This picture has become the symbol of modern anxiety.

Paris, July 1830. For three days Parisians rise up against King Charles the Tenth: the Three Glorious Days. Eugène Delacroix did not fight, but he wanted at least to paint for his country. Liberty, holding the tricolour flag, leads the people over the barricades. Beside her, a boy waves two pistols. The painting was restored at the Louvre in 2024 and has found its colours again.

Florence, around 1485. Sandro Botticelli paints Venus, goddess of love, arriving at the shore standing on a shell. On the left, the wind Zephyr blows her towards land; on the right, a young woman holds out a cloak covered in flowers. It was one of the first large paintings since antiquity to show a mythological subject. It hangs in the Uffizi Gallery in Florence.

Leonardo da Vinci begins this portrait around 1503, in Florence. He never parts with it: he takes it to France, where he spends his last years, and keeps retouching it. His secret is called sfumato: outlines so soft they seem to melt into shadow, especially at the corners of the mouth. That is why her smile seems to change as you look at her. Stolen in 1911 and found two years later, she now lives in the Louvre.
